supplementary_info.identification_information: 100 cm. Huge, blue macaw with yellow facial skin. Intense cobalt blue coloration with black underwings, bare yellow orbital area and lappet bordering the lower mandible. Long tail and huge bill. Immatures have shorter tail and paler yellow bare facial skin. Older adults have lighter grey or white legs. Similar spp. Lear's Macaw A. leari is much smaller and only escaped birds could occur in the range of A. hyacinthinus. Voice Loud, raucous croaking and screeching calls, less harsh than Ara, often given in pairs.

documentation.range: This species occurs in three areas in Brazil: east Amazonia (Pará and Amazonas), the 'Gerais' of Maranhão, Piauí, Bahia, Tocantins, Goiás and Mato Grosso in central Brazil, and in the Pantanal of Mato Grosso, Mato Grosso do Sul and into eastern Bolivia (Santa Cruz), where numbers appear to increase in the dry season perhaps as birds move from Brazil (B. Hennessey in litt. 2012) and Paraguay (a small population in Concepción department [R.P. Clay in litt. 2011, N. López de Kochalka in litt. 2013, H. del Castillo in litt. 2014], with local reports from Alto Paraguay [R.P. Clay in litt. 1997, H. del Castillo in litt. 2014]). The species was formerly more widespread, occurring in parts of Maranhão, Goiás and Mato Grosso where it has not been recorded recently (Presti 2011, Devenish et al. 2021).
documentation.population:
Overall, the population size is likely to have continued to grow since 2003, when it was roughly 4,300 mature individuals based on an estimate of c. 6,500 individuals (Guedes 2004), but the impacts of recent fires in the Pantanal (Santos 2020, Guedes et al. 2021) and a considerable rate of forest cover loss in recent decades (Global Forest Watch 2025) create uncertainty in the trend. Based on updated values for each subpopulation, the population size is placed here in a wider band of 4,700-11,000 mature individuals.

Genetic differences have been found between individuals from the north and south Pantanal, and the Gerais (eastern Mato Grosso, Tocantins and Goias) and northeast populations (northern Brazil), with smaller differences found between the latter two populations (Faria et al. 2008, Almeida 2015, Presti et al. 2015, Almeida et al. 2019), so it is assumed that there are three to four subpopulations. The largest subpopulation is in the south Pantanal, and comprised c. 4,000 individuals (roughly equating to 2,700 mature individuals) and approximately 62% of the total population in 2003 (Guedes 2004). Further surveys in Bolivia in 2008-2011 maintained a population size of between 100 and 300 individuals in the country (Herrera and Davis 2008, Mamani and Estévez 2009, Pinto-Ledezma et al. 2011) but there is no updated estimate of the size of this subpopulation. It was considered to be increasing prior to the recent fires but they may have impacted the population (Guedes et al. 2021), so it is here placed in a wide band of 2,700-7,500 mature individuals. The north Pantanal subpopulation, estimated at around 800-1,000 in 2003 (Guedes 2004) is also likely to have increased and is placed in a band of between 1,000-2,000 mature individuals. The remaining subpopulations totalled around 1,300-1,500 individuals in 2003 with around 500 in northern Brazil and 800-1,000 in central Brazil (Guedes 2004). There is evidence of an expansion of the range and likely population increase in Amazonia (Devenish et al. 2021, WikiAves 2021, eBird 2025) where flocks of up to a hundred have been seen and a minimum of 1,000 individuals present in 2020 (T, Dornas in litt. 2020), and placed in a band of 670-1,000 mature individuals. However in central Brazil the suitable habitat area has declined and records appear to be declining (Devenish et al. 2021, GBIF.org 2025). This is the region with the longest history of habitat conversion and there is also still a level of capture for trade continuing (Presti et al. 2015). The population size here is placed in a precautionary band of 500-800 individuals, roughly equivalent to 330-550 mature individuals. These values sum to a total of 4,700-11,050 mature individuals, rounded for a tentative updated population size of between 4,700-11,000.

In 1987, the global population size was estimated at 2,500-5,000 individuals, with a best estimate placed at around 3,000 (3,219) individuals (Munn et al. 1987). This included c. 1,500 in the Pantanal (including c. 200 individuals in the northern Pantanal, 100-300 in the Bolivian Pantanal, and two individuals in Paraguay), c. 1,000 in the northeast population and c. 750 in the east Amazonian population. This is believed to be when the nadir of the population occurred, with an estimated 10,000 individuals trapped for trade during the 1980s (Collar et al. 2020). It is therefore suspected that the population size in 1978, three generations ago, was a minimum of 10,000 and likely closer to 15,000 individuals.

Counts at a single roosting site, the São Francisco do Perigara ranch in the Mato Grosso part of the Brazilian Pantanal revealed an increase from 234 (95% C. I. = 55) individuals in 2001 to 708 (95% C.I. = 142) individuals in 2015, with a mean rate of increase of 26 individuals per year (Scherer-Neto et al. 2019). Since then, 750 individuals were recorded at the site in 2019, and 736 in 2020 (Guedes et al. 2021) suggesting stability at a higher number and that the increase was in response to favourable management and likely driven by immigration from other regions (Scherer-Neto et al. 2019). Local apparently positive trends in the Pantanal (Scherer-Neto et al. 2019, Guedes et al. 2021) may have been countered by significant threats from the recent unprecedented extent and severity of wildfires in 2019 and 2020 (Santos 2020) which considerably reduced reproductive output (Guedes et al. 2021) and destroyed large areas of the Hyacinth Macaw's main food plants, Attalea phalerata and Acrocomia aculeata (Guedes et al. 2021). In addition high levels of mortality from disease lead to reports of declines from some farmers (A. Lees in litt. 2019).
documentation.habitats: It occurs in várzea and savanna adjacent to tropical forest in east Amazonia, campo cerrado, caatinga and palm-stands in the Gerais, and palm-savannas in the Pantanal. As it prefers forest edges, it tolerates some habitat degradation (Villarroel and Luque 2018), and has been seen in the hundreds in areas of relatively degraded habitat (T. Dornas in litt. 2020). It feeds mostly on the hard fruit of a few regionally endemic palm species (Attalea phalerata and Acrocomia aculeata in the Pantanal [Antas et al. 2006], Maximiliana regia, Orbignya martiana and Astrocaryum in the Amazon region, and Attalea funifera and Syagrus coronata in the northeast of its range [Collar et al. 2020]). It appears to undergo some long-distance seasonal movements, apparently in response to plant phenology (da Silva and Willis 1986), and it may fly long distances between feeding and roosting or nesting sites (Forshaw 1989). Nesting is from July-December in large tree cavities (primarily in Sterculia apetala in the Pantanal [Johnson 1996], and S. pruriens in Amazonia [Presti et al. 2009]) and on cliffs (in the north-east). Two eggs are usually laid, but only one chick normally fledges (C. Yamashita in litt. 2000). The Toco Toucan Ramphastos toco is responsible for dispersing 83% of the seeds of Sterculia apetala hence is key to the availability of nest sites for this species, but is also its main nest predator in the Pantanal (Pizo et al. 2008).
documentation.threats:
There has been massive illegal trade in the species over past decades, with trade increasing rapidly from the 1960s to the 1980s (Munn et al. 1987). At least 10,000 birds were taken from the wild in the 1980s, with 50% destined for the Brazilian market (Mittermeier et al. 1990). In 1983-1984, over 2,500 were flown out of Bahía Negra, Paraguay, with an additional 600 in the late 1980s (J. Pryor in litt. 1998). However, trade in the species declined and was almost halted by the early 2000s (Guedes 2004). Nowadays, trade occurs at low levels (e.g. ten passed through a pet market in Santa Cruz, Bolivia, in August 2004-July 2005 [Herrera and Hennessey 2007]). Recent trade records in Singapore indicated that parrots appeared to be increasing in popularity, and that the Hyacinth Macaw was the most valuable traded bird (Aloysius et al. 2019). Across its range, there is some local hunting and trapping for food and for feathers for use in indigenous handicrafts.

Habitat conversion to agriculture has also contributed to the species' past decline. In the Pantanal, deforestation is ongoing, as forest is converted to pasture, young trees are foraged by cattle, and trees are frequently burned for pasture maintenance (Newton 1994, Junior et al. 2007, Pinto-Ledezma et al. 2011). In the Pantanal, ranchers usually retain palm trees, but destroy other trees, including those used as nesting sites (Munn et al. 1987). In Paraguay, the species' preferred habitats are regarded as seriously threatened (N. López de Kochalka in litt. 2013) and Paso Bravo National Park suffers from illegal logging and hunting activity (H. del Castillo in litt. 2014). In Bolivia, increasing intensification and expansion of grazing and agriculture may be affecting the species (Pinto-Ledezma et al. 2014). In Amazonia, there has been habitat loss for cattle-ranching and hydroelectric power schemes on the rios Tocantins and Xingu (Dornas et al. 2013). The Gerais is being rapidly converted to soya plantations, cattle-ranching and exotic tree plantations (Conservation International 1999).

In 2019 and 2020, the Pantanal was severely affected by wildfires, with over 40,000 km2 (26% of the Brazilian Pantanal) affected in 2020 (Santos 2020), representing a 376% increase compared to the annual average of the area burnt annually in the last two decades (Garcia et al. 2021). The portion of the Pantanal in Mato Grosso state was particularly severely burned, with 41% of the area burned in 2020 (Santos 2020), including the São Francisco do Perigara ranch (Guedes et al. 2021), although the roosting site at the ranch was not burnt (Guedes et al. 2021). At the Refúgio Ecológico Caiman in Mato Grosso do Sul, where the species' largest nesting population occurs, almost half of 98 recorded nests were affected in 2019, with either the nest destroyed by fire, or the loss of chicks or eggs as a result of the heat (Guedes et al. 2021). The fires destroyed large areas of the Hyacinth Macaw's main food plants, Attalea phalerata and Acrocomia aculeata, although some recovery was seen by the following year (Guedes et al. 2021). The severe fires were linked to drought conditions and land use changes, and are expected to increase in frequency as these factors continue (Garcia et al. 2021).

Diseases may also present a threat. From 2015-2018, a total of 177 individuals were found to have died from Herpesvirus in the Brazilian Pantanal, and some farmers reported local population declines (A. Lees in litt. 2019).
documentation.measures:
Conservation Actions Underway
CITES Appendix I and II, protected under Brazilian and Bolivian law and banned from export in all countries of origin. It is managed as part of the Association of Zoos and Aquariums' Parrot Technical Advisory Group. It occurs in a number of protected areas. It is included in the National Action Plan for the Conservation of the Birds of the Cerrado and Pantanal, which includes actions to improve enforcement and run educational activities to curb illegal hunting and trade, improve management of protected areas and monitor impacts of developments, although some of the actions proposed to protect habitat have not been implemented (ICMBio 2023). Many ranch-owners in the Pantanal and in the Gerais no longer permit trappers on their properties. There are several long-term studies and conservation initiatives. In the Brazilian Pantanal, the Hyacinth Macaw Institute has used artificial nests and chick management techniques and raised awareness among cattle ranchers and children (Anon 2004, Corrêa and Guedes 2006). Initiatives involving ecotourism and environmental education have taken place since the 1990s (Collar et al. 2020, Almeida 2015, Villarroel and Luque 2018). Following the Pantanal fires of 2020, supplementary feeding has taken place to compensate for the loss of food trees (Guedes et al. 2021).

Conservation Actions Proposed
Carry out surveys to gain an updated estimate of the population size and to monitor population trends across its range. Monitor domestic and international trade in the species.
Enforce legal measures preventing capture, hunting and trade. Enforce existing laws to promote habitat conservation, including compensation for ecological services (J.N. Pinto-Ledezma in litt. 2020). Continue education programmes to discourage destruction of forest patches (Pinho and Nogeira 2003). Improve capacity and coordination of fire management and control in the Pantanal.
documentation.use_trade:
There continues to be a low level of illegal capture of the species for the cage bird trade (Presti et al. 2015). Recent trade records in Singapore indicated that parrots appeared to be increasing in popularity, and that the Hyacinth Macaw was the most valuable traded bird (Aloysius et al. 2019). Across its range, there is some local hunting and trapping for food and for feathers for use in indigenous handicrafts.

Previously there was massive illegal trade in the species. Trade increased rapidly from the 1960s to the 1980s (Munn et al. 1987). At least 10,000 birds were taken from the wild in the 1980s, with half destined for the Brazilian market (Mittermeier et al. 1990). In 1983-1984, over 2,500 were flown out of Bahía Negra, Paraguay, with an additional 600 in the late 1980s (J. Pryor in litt. 1998). However, trade in the species declined and was almost halted by the early 2000s (Guedes 2004). Nowadays, trade occurs at low levels (e.g. ten passed through a pet market in Santa Cruz, Bolivia, in August 2004-July 2005 [Herrera and Hennessey 2007]) and genetic methods were used to determine the source area for confiscated birds in the 2010s (Presti et al. 2015).
documentation.rationale: This spectacular and charismatic species suffered a very rapid population reduction due largely to unsustainable trapping for the cage bird trade, but enforcement and dedicated conservation action has reduced illegal take and allowed a significant recovery in the population since a low point in the late 1980s. Even so, this very long-lived species' population may still be less than half the size it was three generations ago, just before the most severe exploitation took place, hence it is assessed as Vulnerable. There remains a risk that the species is once again targeted unsustainably and the continuation of conservation action and expansion of monitoring effort is needed to sustain the species' recovery.
documentation.trend_justification:
Throughout the 1980s the species suffered major declines as an estimated 10,000 birds were illegally captured for the pet trade and widespread habitat destruction and hunting caused a further reduction in numbers (Anon. 2004, Collar et al. 2020). Based on the past (10,000-15,000 mature individuals in 1978) and current population sizes (4,700-11,000) calculated for this assessment (see Population) the overall rate of reduction for the past three generations (46.8 years) is suspected to fall between 27.6% and 54.4%.

It is clear from the recorded recovery that the reduction in population size is reversible, and also that the driver has been correctly identified as unsustainable exploitation for the cage bird trade. While there is an ongoing low level of illegal take from the wild in the Pantanal and Cerrado at least (Presti et al. 2015), recovery in the population size has taken place with this rate ongoing, hence the level is currently deemed insufficient to have caused further declines over the past three generations.

The three generation rate of reduction falls rapidly as the start year moves into the period that the population was itself falling rapidly in the 1980s, and the fastest rate that includes both the future and the past is the shortest extension into the future, 1979 to 2026, at 14% to 40%. Potentially rates of reduction could begin to increase again in the future, but currently the balance of benefit to the species from opening up intact forest versus the further clearance of already altered forest habitats and the potential for rates of illegal take to increase is too uncertain to quantify with current data.

The total area of modelled suitable habitat has increased between 1995 and 2019 (Devenish et al. 2021). Increases were most evident in north Brazil along Amazonian rivers (which appears to be a positive response to the initial clearance of intact forest), but were also recorded in the Pantanal, although subsequent large fires may have reversed this at least temporarily (Santos 2020, Guedes et al. 2021). This habitat increase has come during a period where rates of forest cover loss within the range have been rapid. From 2001 to 2020, approximately 17% of tree cover with at least 30% canopy cover was lost from within the species' range (Global Forest Watch 2021). Extrapolated forward over three generations from 2000, this would equate to 40% loss of tree cover if tree cover loss continued at the same area per year. This apparently contradictory habitat trend is explained by the species favouring forest edges and there have been reported sightings of flocks of hundreds of individuals in relatively degraded habitat (T. Dornas in litt. 2020). However, there is a threshold level of clearance that results in rapid loss of the species from an area (Devenish et al. 2021). This implies that continuing tree cover loss, especially the further conversion to large scale cropland or cattle ranching, will eventually result in population declines but that the magnitude of these depends on the balance of recent clearance versus further conversion of degraded but forested land to a largely treeless landscape (Devenish et al. 2021). The species does rely on large trees for nesting, roosting and feeding. Hence while recent trends appear to be increasing, there is the potential for habitat loss to drive future declines. It is inferred that there is a continuing decline based on the high likelihood that the habitat changes ongoing will translate into future population declines, despite recent population recovery and expansion into newly cleared sites.

In 2019 and 2020, the Pantanal was severely affected by wildfires, with over 40,000 km (26% of the Brazilian Pantanal) affected in 2020 (Santos 2020), representing a 376% increase compared to the annual average of the area burnt annually in the last two decades (Garcia et al. 2021). The portion of the Pantanal in Mato Grosso state was particularly severely burned, with 41% of the area burned in 2020 (Santos 2020), including the São Francisco do Perigara ranch (Guedes et al. 2021), although the roosting site at the ranch was not burnt (Guedes et al. 2021). At the Refúgio Ecológico Caiman in Mato Grosso do Sul, where the species' largest nesting population occurs, almost half of 98 recorded nests were affected in 2019, with either the nest destroyed by fire, or the loss of chicks or eggs as a result of the heat (Guedes 2021). The fires destroyed large areas of the Hyacinth Macaw's main food plants, Attalea phalerata and Acrocomia aculeata, although some recovery was seen by the following year (Guedes et al. 2021). The impact of the fires on the species' population size is not known. The severe fires were linked to drought conditions and land use changes, and are expected to increase in frequency as these factors continue (Garcia et al. 2021).

There is little recent direct survey information on trends in the population. Counts at a single roosting site, the São Francisco do Perigara ranch in the Mato Grosso part of the Brazilian Pantanal, revealed an increase from 234 (95% C. I. = 55) individuals in 2001 to 708 (95% C. I. = 142) individuals in 2015, with a mean rate of increase of 26 individuals per year (Scherer-Neto et al. 2019). Since then, 750 individuals were recorded at the site in 2019, and 736 in 2020 (Guedes et al. 2021). This rate of increase may not have been representative of the wider population, as the the ranch management in the area of the roosting site may have been particularly favourable to the species, and there may have been immigration from other regions (Scherer-Neto et al. 2019). From 2015-2018, a total of 177 individuals were found to have died from Herpesvirus in the Brazilian Pantanal, and some farmers reported local population declines (A. Lees in litt. 2019), but there doesn't appear to have been an overall population impact.
